opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think simulation is incredibly powerful, but it has some real weaknesses that we have to be honest about.

The first and most famous one is the sim-to-real gap. Physics engines are approximations. Things like contact dynamics, friction, deformable objects, cloth, fluids, those are really hard to simulate accurately. If you're doing something simple, like a robot dog walking on terrain, you can get away with it, and we've seen amazing sim-to-real transfer for locomotion. But once you get into dexterous manipulation, where fingers are touching objects and things slide and deform in subtle ways, the simulation starts to diverge from reality, and policies trained purely in sim can break when they hit the real world.

The second weakness is diversity and content. To train a generalist robot, you need a huge variety of environments, objects, textures, lighting, and tasks. And traditionally, all of that has to be built by hand. Someone has to create the 3D assets, design the scenes, write the reward functions or the task specifications. That doesn't scale nearly as well as people sometimes assume. So even though simulation runs fast, you're bottlenecked by how much interesting content humans can author.

Third, there's the visual gap. Rendered images often don't look like real camera images, so if your policy relies on vision, you have to deal with that domain shift too.

The tricks we use to mitigate these are things like domain randomization, where you vary physical parameters and visuals so much that the real world looks like just another variation. And increasingly, I'm excited about generative models, using video generation and world models as a kind of neural simulation, to fill in the diversity and realism that classical graphics pipelines struggle with.

But the bottom line is that I don't think simulation alone gets you all the way. You need a mix: real-world teleoperation data, which is high quality but expensive and doesn't scale; internet video data, which is massive but has no action labels; and simulation data, which is scalable but has these gaps. The real art is figuring out how to combine all three into one data pyramid.

r001.rationale: The response describes physics and visual gaps and says simulation alone is insufficient, but does not state that improving simulation graphics cannot fully eliminate the simulation-to-reality gap.

r002.rationale: It says generalist robots need a huge variety of environments, objects, and tasks, while simulation content is traditionally hand-built and does not scale well.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I'm a huge believer in simulation, but I want to be honest about where it breaks down, because the failure modes are really specific.

The first one is the sim-to-real gap, and it's actually two gaps, not one. There's the physics gap and the perception gap. On the physics side, simulators are pretty good at rigid bodies. A cube, a table, a robot arm with known joint limits, those are easy. The moment you get into contact-rich manipulation, deformables, fluids, friction that changes depending on whether the surface is slightly oily, the simulator just starts lying to you. A robot can learn a beautiful policy for folding a towel in simulation, and that towel behaves nothing like a real towel. Cloth, cables, food, soft tissue, those are exactly the things humans do all day, and they're exactly the things physics engines are worst at.

The perception gap is the other half. You can render photorealistic scenes now, and that's gotten dramatically better with generative models, but photorealism is not the same as matching the real distribution. Real cameras have motion blur, rolling shutter, weird exposure, lens dirt. Real homes have clutter that no one would ever author as a 3D asset. So you end up doing massive domain randomization, which works, but it's a bit of a hack. You're basically telling the model "don't trust anything specific," which costs you sample efficiency.

The second weakness is what I'd call the diversity problem. Simulation gives you unlimited quantity, but the quantity is only as diverse as the assets and scenes you've built. If you have a thousand objects in your asset library, you have a thousand objects, no matter how many trajectories you generate. So people sometimes confuse "infinite data" with "infinite information," and those are not the same thing. The long tail of the real world, the weird mug handle, the drawer that sticks, is really hard to author by hand.

Third, and this is subtle, simulation requires you to specify the task and the reward. In the real world, data collected by humans has the task implicitly baked in. In sim, someone has to write down what success means, and reward hacking is the default behavior of RL. The robot will find the one physics bug that lets it clip through the table and get the reward.

So my view is that sim is not a replacement for real data, it's a multiplier on it. Real-world data anchors the distribution, simulation lets you scale coverage and practice the dangerous or rare stuff. And the thing that's changing the equation is that generative models are starting to become the simulator, learned world models rather than hand-coded physics, which attacks the diversity and asset-authoring problems directly. That's where I think the long-term answer lives.

r001.rationale: It says photorealism is not the same as matching the real distribution and describes camera and scene differences that sustain the perception gap.

r002.rationale: It says simulated diversity is limited by authored assets and scenes, while the real world has a difficult-to-author long tail of objects and situations.

astra-6.text:
The biggest weakness is the gap between simulation and reality. In a simulator, you can generate enormous amounts of data, but that data is only as good as the world you’ve modeled. If the physics is wrong, your robot can become very good at solving the wrong problem.

Contact is particularly difficult: friction, slipping, deformable objects, cables, fabric. Those interactions are hard to simulate accurately, and small errors can change whether a manipulation task succeeds. A policy can also exploit quirks of the simulator that simply don’t exist in the real world.

Then there’s diversity. You can randomize lighting, textures, and object positions, but you’re still choosing what to randomize. Reality will introduce things you didn’t anticipate.

So I think simulation is extremely useful for scaling practice, but you need a feedback loop with the real world. Test the policy, identify where it fails, and use those failures to improve the simulator and the training distribution. Generating more data alone doesn’t close that gap.

r001.rationale: The response describes limitations in physics, contact, and randomized visual settings, but does not clearly state that improving simulation graphics cannot fully eliminate the simulation-to-reality gap.

r002.rationale: The response says simulated diversity is limited by what developers choose to randomize, while reality introduces scenarios they did not anticipate.

sol-6.1.text:
The biggest weakness is the gap between what you simulate and what actually happens in the real world. In simulation, you control the physics, the sensors, the objects. But those models are approximations. A policy can become very good at exploiting the simulator without learning something that transfers to a real robot.

Contact is particularly challenging. Think about grasping a slippery object, manipulating cloth, or plugging in a cable. Small differences in friction, deformation, or timing can completely change the outcome. Making an image look realistic doesn’t necessarily make those interactions physically accurate.

There’s also a coverage problem. You can generate a huge amount of simulation data, but someone still has to decide which environments, objects, and tasks to generate. Scale alone doesn’t guarantee diversity.

So I see simulation as a powerful way to learn and explore, but you still need real-world data and real-world testing to find out where your assumptions break.

r001.rationale: The response says realistic-looking images do not ensure physically accurate interactions, within its discussion of the simulation-to-reality gap. This communicates that better graphics alone cannot eliminate the gap.

r002.rationale: The response notes that simulation data may lack diversity because people choose which scenarios to generate, but it does not clearly compare that coverage with the broader scenarios robots encounter in the real world.
